result.reasoning: Emergency conservative pipeline requires system design for reliability, DevOps for pipeline configuration, security-first defaults, and quality assurance enforcement.

key_risks: Heavy dependency on unbuilt features (#43 team-based stages, #44 autonomous PM agent) — cannot implement without them
Race conditions and state corruption when spawning/dismissing agents mid-pipeline while other agents hold file locks or are mid-edit
Context transfer to new agents is lossy — late-joining agents may lack critical reasoning context that accumulated over iterations
Budget-aware scaling adds circular complexity: cost tracking must be real-time accurate while scaling decisions happen concurrently
Cooldown logic and thrashing prevention are hard to tune — too aggressive wastes resources, too conservative defeats the purpose
tmux pane management for dynamic spawn/dismiss is fragile — pane IDs shift, windows resize, and cleanup of dismissed agent panes can leave orphans
implementation_hints: Implement as an extension to sw-pipeline.sh with a new sw-team-scaler.sh module that the PM agent calls — keep scaling logic separate from pipeline orchestration
Use file-based signaling (e.g., .claude/pipeline-artifacts/scale-requests.json) for scale-up/down requests to avoid race conditions with direct tmux manipulation
Start with scale-up only (adding agents) — scale-down (dismissing agents) is much harder due to in-flight work and should be phase 2
Context transfer should reuse the existing memory system (sw-memory.sh) plus pipeline-state.md rather than inventing a new context protocol
Build and test the cooldown mechanism with a simple time-based lock file before adding sophisticated thrashing detection
Mock all scaling triggers in tests — create sw-team-scaler-test.sh with simulated build failures, coverage gaps, and budget exhaustion scenarios

Implement dark mode with CSS custom properties and a React context provider for theme state

complexity_assessment.reasoning: Well-specified configuration work with clear acceptance criteria; complexity is in coordinating template structure, CLI integration, and test validation rather than algorithmic difficulty

skill_rationale.architecture-design: Create an ADR documenting the emergency template design rationale—why 2x timeouts, opus-only routing, and disabled intelligence are the right conservative tradeoffs for reliability
skill_rationale.brainstorming: Challenge assumptions: does disabling intelligence actually improve reliability, or does it remove useful safety checks? Are 50% more iterations the right knob to turn?
skill_rationale.deploy-safety: Emergency template is a fallback mechanism for platform reliability crises, so must be designed with predictable, observable behavior and clear failure modes
skill_rationale.adversarial-quality: Test failure scenarios: what breaks if opus hits rate limits? If checkpoints corrupt? If doubling timeouts still isn't enough? Find the template's limits
skill_rationale.security-audit: Verify disabling intelligence/prediction doesn't inadvertently bypass security checks, architecture validation, or other safety gates critical to reliable operation
skill_rationale.testing-strategy: Design test suite covering all acceptance criteria: timeout scaling validation, model routing force, checkpoint behavior, iteration limits, verbose logging output
skill_rationale.validation-thoroughness: Validate beyond tests that emergency template actually delivers claimed reliability improvements under realistic failure conditions, not just happy path execution
skill_rationale.pr-quality: Communicate the purpose, tradeoffs (slower/costlier but more reliable), and when to activate emergency template so teams use it appropriately
skill_rationale.documentation: Update CLAUDE.md Pipeline Templates section with emergency template entry, usage guidance, and rationale for when this fallback should be activated
